messages.subject: [R-sig-ME] Random-effects structure for a volleyball tactics model (crossed vs. nested)
messages.subject_clean: Random-effects structure for a volleyball tactics model (crossed vs. nested)
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am analysing a volleyball dataset in which a tactic (secret ?), ordered
by the coach, is executed by one player.

The outcome is binary (WIN / LOSS).

Each observation (row of data) involves exactly one coach and one player,
and the data were collected across matches over three seasons.

The fixed effects will be MATCH_STATUS, SET_STATUS, SEX and DIVISION.

I am unsure about the random-effects structure. Which of these is more
appropriate?

   1. Crossed effects: (1 | COACH) + (1 | PLAYER) + (1 | MATCH)
   2. Nested effects: (1 | MATCH/COACH) + (1 | MATCH/PLAYER)

Thank you in advance for your help.

Best

messages.subject: [R-sig-ME]  Random-effects structure for a volleyball tactics model (crossed vs. nested)
messages.subject_clean: Random-effects structure for a volleyball tactics model (crossed vs. nested)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jorge,

Check this:
https://bbolker.github.io/mixedmodels-misc/glmmFAQ.html#nested-or-crossed

Presumably you'd want crossed effects here, because otherwise you lose a
random effect that captures the fact that PLAYER A within MATCH 1 is the
same player as PLAYER A within MATCH 2.
(1 | MATCH/PLAYER) is the same as (1 | MATCH) + (1 | MATCH:PLAYER), so you
can see that you'd only get random intercepts for MATCHes and for the
MATCH:PLAYER unique *combinations*.

(note that this also depends on the way PLAYER is coded; if PLAYERs get
different codes on different matches, then crossed or nested would be
identical)

João

messages.subject: [R-sig-ME] Hierarchical Generalized Additive Models in R – Live Online Course | 8–11 February 2027
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical Generalized Additive Models in R – Live Online Course | 8–11 February 2027
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

PR Stats is pleased to announce an upcoming live online course that may be of interest to members of the R-SIG-Mixed-Models mailing list.

Hierarchical Generalized Additive Models for Biological Sciences (HGAM01)

Dates: 8?11 February 2027
Duration: 22 hours (4 days)
Format: Live Online via Zoom
Instructor: Dr Gavin Simpson
Course Fee: ?400

Hierarchical Generalized Additive Models (HGAMs) extend the flexibility of Generalized Additive Models to grouped and hierarchical data, allowing nonlinear relationships to vary between groups while accounting for shared structure.

For researchers familiar with mixed-effects models, HGAMs provide a useful framework for modelling nonlinear trends across individuals, sites, populations or experimental groups, using penalised smooths and random-effect structures.

This practical course will focus on fitting, interpreting and evaluating HGAMs in R using the mgcv package.

Topics covered include:

  *   Shared and group-specific nonlinear smooths.

  *   Factor?smooth interactions and hierarchical GAM structures.

  *   Random effects, smoothing penalties and partial pooling.

  *   Alternative parameterisations, including fs and sz smooths.

  *   Modelling heterogeneity between groups.

  *   Model diagnostics, inference and uncertainty.

  *   Visualising and interpreting hierarchical nonlinear relationships.

Who should attend?

The course is aimed at PhD students, postdoctoral researchers and applied statisticians working with grouped, repeated-measures or hierarchical datasets, particularly those interested in extending conventional mixed-effects modelling to nonlinear relationships.

Participants should have experience with R and regression modelling. Prior familiarity with GAMs is strongly recommended.

Recordings and course materials

All sessions will be recorded and made available to participants. R scripts, datasets and supporting materials will also be provided.

Full details and registration:

https://prstats.org/course/hierarchical-generalized-additive-models-for-biological-sciences-hgam01/

Please feel free to share this announcement with colleagues, students, research groups or others who may find it useful.

Best wishes,

Oliver Hooker
Managing Partner
PR Stats
https://prstats.org<https://prstats.org/>


Sent from Outlook for Mac
